hints: First sort the dark spaces in Fig. 4.1 by size - pick out the very large wide open circles and then look for clusters of much smaller thin-walled circles packed between them.
walkthrough:
Read the Micrograph by Size**
Think of Fig. 4.1 as a transverse section through a vascular bundle. The very large open lumens are xylem vessels built for carrying lots of water. Phloem sieve tubes are much narrower because they carry concentrated sugar solution under pressure, not a fast transpiration stream.

Pick the Correct Cluster**
Find a group of small, similar-sized, thin-walled cells sitting between the big xylem vessels. Draw a clear label line with a ruler to the wall or the lumen of one of those small cells and write phloem sieve tube.
Final answer: Label line to the wall or lumen of any small phloem sieve tube.

hints: Think about what a leaf makes in photosynthesis that a non-photosynthetic root or growing fruit cannot make for itself.
Now link that substance to direction of movement - from where it is made or stored to where it is used - and recall the special name for bulk flow in phloem.
walkthrough:
What Is Carried**
Phloem sieve tubes are living tubes for food, not water. They carry assimilates made by the plant, mainly sucrose plus amino acids, auxins and other solutes.

Where To and How**
Movement is from source to sink, for example from leaves to roots, fruits, seeds and growing buds. This bidirectional bulk transport is called translocation by mass flow.
Final answer: Transport of assimilates, e.g. sucrose and amino acids, from source to sink by translocation / mass flow.

hints: Focus on what is added to the wall during differentiation - a very strong, waterproof polymer that is not present in ordinary parenchyma walls.
Think why a tube carrying water under strong tension pull from transpiration must be both waterproof and rigid enough not to collapse inward.
Then think about the cellulose part of the wall and the gaps left in the thickening - how do they help water stick and move sideways?
walkthrough:
Lignin for Waterproofing and Strength**
As the vessel element differentiates it deposits lignin. Lignin is waterproof so water stays inside the lumen instead of leaking out through the wall. It is also very rigid and strong.

Resisting Collapse**
Xylem sap is pulled up under tension, which tends to suck the wall inward. The lignified wall supports the vessel and the whole stem and prevents inward collapse.

Cellulose, Pits and Growth**
The cellulose microfibrils are hydrophilic and form hydrogen bonds with water, so water adheres to the wall and is helped to move up. Unthickened pits are left in the lignin to allow lateral movement of water between vessels. In young growing regions annular rings or spirals of lignin allow the vessel to stretch with extension growth.

Final answer: Lignified walls waterproof the vessel; lignin gives support and prevents inward collapse under tension; cellulose allows adhesion of water by hydrogen bonding to aid water flow; pits allow lateral movement of water; rings / spirals allow extension / growth.

hints: Start with the shape - a cube has 6 identical square faces, so work out the area of one face of side 0.1 m first.
Next recall the volume of a cube is length x width x height, all 0.1 m here, and watch the powers of 10.
Finally divide your total surface area by your volume to get the ratio and leave the units as a simple number.
walkthrough:
Calculate Surface Area**
For a cube: $\text{surface area} = 6 \times l^2$. So $\text{surface area} = 6 \times 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.06 \text{ m}^2$.

Calculate Volume**
For a cube: $\text{volume} = l^3$. So $\text{volume} = 0.1 \times 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.001 \text{ m}^3$, which is $1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$.

Divide to Get the Ratio**
$\text{ratio} = \text{surface area} / \text{volume} = 0.06 / 0.001 = 60$. Always show each step clearly to gain full credit.
Final answer: surface area $= 0.1 \times 0.1 \times 6 = 0.06 \text{ m}^2$; volume $= 0.1 \times 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.001 \text{ m}^3$; surface area to volume ratio $= 0.06 / 0.001 = 60$.

hints: Think what a small surface area compared to a large volume means for diffusion - a long distance from the surface to deep cells and only a small entry area for the needs of many cells.
Now connect that limit to the solution - how does a branched transport system carrying materials deep inside the body solve distance and speed?
walkthrough:
Why Diffusion Fails When Large**
As size increases, volume and demand grow faster than surface area for uptake. Distances from the surface to inner cells become long, so diffusion alone is too slow to supply oxygen and nutrients and remove wastes.

How a Transport System Helps**
A mass transport system such as blood carries materials rapidly through branched vessels deep into the body, bringing them close to every cell so that the final diffusion distance is short.
Final answer: Diffusion over the body surface / to inner cells is too slow to meet needs over long distances; a transport system delivers materials more quickly and takes materials close to cells.
